processing: Handled in the usual Darjeeling way for black tea: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, with lighter oxidation in spring.
harvest_season: As across Darjeeling, first flush in spring, second flush in early summer and an autumn picking.
appearance_dry: Typical of high Darjeeling whole-leaf tea: wiry leaf in mixed greens and browns, with paler tips in fine lots.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in spring lots, deepening to amber in summer lots.
appearance_wet: Mixed green and coppery leaf, depending on the flush.
taste_profile: No fixed house taste is well documented. Typical of high Darjeeling, expect floral lift and briskness in spring and more fruit and body in summer.

brewing.notes: Western style. Go cooler and shorter with spring lots; second flush takes hotter water.

vintage_note: Sold as named lots by flush and year, including invoice-style names such as Red Thunder Gold. Most of the premium output is exported. As with other Darjeeling teas, spring lots are for drinking within about a year of harvest, so check the year.
description:
Gopaldhara sits in the Mirik block and counts among the highest gardens in Darjeeling, with most of its land between 5,500 and 7,000 feet. Of 320 hectares, 172 are planted with tea. The name joins Gopal, the man who owned the original paddy fields, with dhara, Nepali for a small stream.

The method is the normal Darjeeling one, with altitude and season doing the shaping. Cool, cloudy high ground is generally credited with slowing growth and holding aroma, which is why gardens at this height are prized.

Brew it like any good Darjeeling, Western style, and do not over-steep a spring lot. Taste notes vary by lot and little is documented about a fixed character, so read the description for the specific batch and trust your own cup.

Most of the premium tea goes abroad, sometimes under lot names such as Red Thunder Gold. A lot name is a seller's label, so look for the flush and year beside it.
history:
The plantation dates from 1881, developed on those paddy fields. It was bought by a man named Kingslay in 1920, passed to Moolji Sikka and Company in 1947, and was bought by Dalchand Saria in 1953 to 1954.

His son Shiv Saria and grandson Hrishikesh Saria were managing it as of 2020 under the Sona Tea Group, which also runs Rohini in Darjeeling and two estates in the Dooars.
